'''Alan Howard Ward''' [[Order of the British Empire|OBE]] (28 July 1925 – 2 December 2021) was a physicist who influenced science education in Africa and contributed to the understanding of the impacts of radioactive chemicals on human health.

== Education and early years ==

Alan was the youngest of four children of Edward Howard Ward, a post office worker, and Ursula Mabel Ward (née Vale). He was born in [[Woodford, London|Woodford]], London. He attended [[Forest School, Walthamstow|The Forest School]] in Waltham Forest until 1937. The family later moved to Chichester where he attended [[Chichester High School For Boys|Chichester High School for Boys]]. Following a wartime degree at the [[University of Birmingham]] he worked under [[Mark Oliphant]] and completed a PhD in 1949.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Ward|first1=A. H.|title=Directional-correlation in radioactivity|url=https://birmingham-primo.hosted.exlibrisgroup.com/permalink/f/vmc2c6/44BIR_ALMA_DS2198123110004871|access-date=3 January 2022|website=University of Birmingham Library}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Ward|first1=A. H.|last2=Walker|first2=D.|date=1949|title=Directional Correlation between Successive Internal-Conversion Electrons from Tantalum-181*|journal=Nature|language=en|volume=163|issue=4135|pages=168|doi=10.1038/163168a0|s2cid=4063677 |issn=1476-4687|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Bunyan|first1=D E|last2=Lundby|first2=A|last3=Ward|first3=A H|last4=Walker|first4=D|date=1948-10-01|title=The Delayed Coincidence Method in the Study of Radioactivity, with Application to Isomerism in181Ta|url=https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/0959-5309/61/4/302|journal=Proceedings of the Physical Society|language=en|volume=61|issue=4|pages=300–306|doi=10.1088/0959-5309/61/4/302|issn=0959-5309|url-access=subscription}}</ref> Alongside his studies, he served with the [[Air Training Corps]] from 20 September 1941 to 1 August 1943, where he was trained as a Flight Mechanic, and served with the [[Home Guard (United Kingdom)|Home Guard]] from 6 October 1943 to 31 December 1944. As part of the Birmingham University Senior Training Corps, he obtained the War Certificate "A" in 1944 and "B" in Electrical and Mechanical Engineering in 1945.

== Career ==

=== Finsen Institute, Denmark ===
After a period as an Assistant Lecturer at the University of Birmingham, Ward was sent by the [[Atomic Energy Research Establishment]] to study [[Thorotrast]] poisoning at the [[:da:Finseninstituttet|Finsen Institute]] in Denmark for two years. This work involved following up on patients who had been injected with Thorotrast as a [[radiocontrast agent]] in [[medical radiography]], and started his interest in medical physics.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Ward|first1=A. H.|last2=Jensen|first2=P. G.|date=1951|title=Measurement of Radioactivity in Human Breath|journal=Nature|language=en|volume=167|issue=4250|pages=600|doi=10.1038/167600a0|pmid=14826863 |issn=1476-4687|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Rundo|first1=J|last2=Ward|first2=A H|last3=Jensen|first3=P G|date=1958-10-01|title=Measurement of Thoron in the Breath|url=https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/0031-9155/3/2/301|journal=Physics in Medicine and Biology|language=en|volume=3|issue=2|pages=101–110|doi=10.1088/0031-9155/3/2/301|pmid=13601139|s2cid=250745133|issn=0031-9155|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

=== University of Ghana ===

Following an interview by the Inter-University Council for Higher Education Overseas (ICHEO),<ref>{{Cite journal|date=1946-03-01|title=Inter-University Council for Higher Education in the Colonies|journal=Nature|language=en|volume=157|issue=3985|pages=347|doi=10.1038/157347a0|s2cid=4104076 |issn=1476-4687|doi-access=free}}</ref> Ward was appointed as a lecturer in physics at the University of Ghana in 1951. For the period 1956-59 he served as Secretary of the Ghana National Committee for the [[International Geophysical Year]]. He was made a Senior Lecturer in 1958, and associate professor in 1963. He represented Ghana at the "Atoms for peace" conference in Geneva in 1959, and at Commonwealth Atomic Scientists and IAEA meetings.

==== Retention and toxicity of Strontium-90 ====

Starting in 1959, Ward founded a University Radioisotope and Health Physics Unit in Ghana with support from the Government National Research Council (later the [[Ghana Academy of Arts and Sciences]]) and the [[International Atomic Energy Agency]] (IAEA). With support from the Radiochemical Centre in Amersham (later [[Amersham plc]]) and the [[Atomic Energy Research Establishment]] at Harwell, he carried out long-term experiments on the effects of low doses of [[Strontium-90]] on monkeys.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Edington|first1=G. M.|last2=Judd|first2=J. M.|last3=Ward|first3=A. H.|date=1955|title=Delayed Toxicity of Radiostrontium in Monkeys|journal=Nature|language=en|volume=175|issue=4444|pages=33|doi=10.1038/175033a0|pmid=13223785 |s2cid=4274808 |issn=1476-4687|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Edington|first1=G. M.|last2=Ward|first2=A. H.|last3=Judd|first3=J. M.|last4=Mole|first4=R. H.|date=1956|title=The acute lethal effects in monkeys of radiostrontium|url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/path.1700710203|journal=The Journal of Pathology and Bacteriology|language=en|volume=71|issue=2|pages=277–293|doi=10.1002/path.1700710203|pmid=13398874 |issn=1555-2039|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Edington|first1=G. M.|last2=Judd|first2=J. M.|last3=Ward|first3=A. H.|date=1953|title=Toxicity of Radiostrontium in Monkeys|url=https://www.nature.com/articles/172122b0|journal=Nature|language=en|volume=172|issue=4368|pages=122–123|doi=10.1038/172122b0|pmid=13072599 |s2cid=4296621 |issn=1476-4687|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Mole|first1=R. H.|last2=Ward|first2=A. H.|date=1970|title=Yttrium-90 in Gonads of Monkeys containing Strontium-90|journal=Nature|language=en|volume=226|issue=5241|pages=175|doi=10.1038/226175a0|pmid=4985388 |s2cid=4210979 |issn=1476-4687|doi-access=free}}</ref> Some of these results were presented at the UNESCO International Conference on Radioisotopes in Scientific Research in 1957. The unit also used radioisotopes to track [[dimethoate]] in the commercially important [[Theobroma cacao|cacao trees]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Dunn|first1=E.|last2=Ward|first2=A. H.|date=1965|title=The movement of 32 phosphorus - labelled dimethoate in the cacao tree, Theobroma cacao L.|url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/j.1744-7348.1965.tb01260.x|journal=Annals of Applied Biology|language=en|volume=56|issue=3|pages=419–428|doi=10.1111/j.1744-7348.1965.tb01260.x|issn=1744-7348|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

==== Atomic bomb tests ====

In advance of the [[Gerboise Bleue (nuclear test)|Gerboise Bleue]] French atomic bomb test in Algeria, Ward initiated radioactive fallout measurements across Ghana, and worked with the Ministry of Defence to build and staff dedicated laboratories in both [[Legon]] and Northern Ghana. His results on the level of radioactive fallout were contested by the French Government, who sent military officers to inspect the laboratories and verify the results. The results were presented to President [[Kwame Nkrumah]]'s government, contributing to the decision to cut off diplomatic relations with France.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Ward|first1=A. H.|last2=Marr|first2=J. D.|date=1960|title=Radioactive Fall-Out in Ghana|url=https://www.nature.com/articles/187299a0|journal=Nature|language=en|volume=187|issue=4734|pages=299–300|doi=10.1038/187299a0|pmid=13842861 |s2cid=4210258 |issn=1476-4687|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

==== Proposed nuclear reactor at Kwabenya ====

President Nkrumah asked [[Robert Patrick Baffour]], then Vice-Chancellor of the Kumasi College of Science and Technology (later the [[Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology]]), to head up an initiative to establish a nuclear power program for Ghana. This later led to a proposal that Ghana import an IRT 2000 nuclear research reactor<ref>{{Cite book|title=Directory Of Nuclear Reactors, Vol. Iii: Research, Test And Experimental Reactors. (Soviet Research Reactor Irt)|publisher=International Atomic Energy Agency|year=1960|location=Vienna|pages=29–45}}</ref> from the Soviet Union by 1964 and install it at [[Kwabenya]]. Ward, as head of the Radioisotopes and Health Physics Unit at Legon, estimated that Ghana needed approximately sixty "top-level Ghanaian scientists" and that it was not feasible to meet those needs.<ref>Letter from A.H. Ward, Acting Director, Radioisotope and Health Physics Unit, University of Ghana at Legon to Dr Wilson, 29 January 1963. Held in Public Records And Archives Administration Department for Ghana Atomic Energy Commission, 1963-64.</ref> Nkrumah decided as a result that Ward was not fully supportive of his plans for nuclear research collaboration with the Soviet Union, so had him replaced by [[Alan Nunn May]].<ref>{{Cite book|last=Osseo-Asare|first=Abena Dove|url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/atomic-junction/908C8667C97132B19B3DA93B90BCD41A|title=Atomic Junction: Nuclear Power in Africa after Independence|date=2019|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-1-108-47124-4|location=Cambridge|doi=10.1017/9781108557955|s2cid=204186038 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Allman|first=Jean|date=2008-06-13|title=Nuclear Imperialism and the Pan-African Struggle for Peace and Freedom: Ghana, 1959–1962|url=https://doi.org/10.1080/10999940802115419|journal=Souls|volume=10|issue=2|pages=83–102|doi=10.1080/10999940802115419|s2cid=144174169 |issn=1099-9949|url-access=subscription}}</ref> This led to Ward leaving Ghana at the end of 1965.

=== UNZA ===

Ward was appointed as Professor of Physics at the [[University of Zambia]] (UNZA) in 1965, where he helped to found the department. He continued research on medical physics and remained there until 1975.{{citation needed|date=May 2025}}

=== University of Swaziland ===

Ward joined the [[University of Botswana, Lesotho and Swaziland|University of Botswana, Lesotho, and Swaziland]] (UBLS, later the [[University of Botswana and Swaziland]] and now the [[University of Eswatini|University of eSwatini]]) at the start of 1976. Reflecting the initial specialization of the university in agriculture, his research direction turned to the applications of physics to commercial farming. During his time in Swaziland he was awarded an OBE for services to science education in Africa.

=== Retirement ===

Ward retired to the United Kingdom in 1986. During his retirement he worked as a Physics Associate Lecturer with the [[Open University]] and taught with the [[University of the Third Age]] (U3A). As part of a wider interest in climate change, he adapted, built, and used electric vehicles, and became chair of the Battery Vehicle Society.

== Physics texts adapted for Africa ==

During their time in Ghana, Ward's wife E. H. Ward wrote a physics text covering the high school curriculum and adapted for an African audience.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Ward|first=E. H.|title=Senior Physics 1|publisher=[[Thomas Nelson (publisher)|Nelson]]|year=1965|location=London|language=English}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|last=Ward|first=E. H.|title=Senior Physics 2|publisher=[[Thomas Nelson (publisher)|Nelson]]|year=1965|location=London|language=English}}</ref> This used images and examples from Ghana to illustrate physical concepts, and appeared in a "Science for Tropical Secondary Schools" series. Alan Ward later collaborated with his wife to update the books to use [[International System of Units|S.I. units]] and update some of the contents.<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Ward|first1=E. H.|title=Mechanics|last2=Ward|first2=A. H.|publisher=[[Thomas Nelson (publisher)|Nelson]]|year=1977|location=London|language=English}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|last1=Ward|first1=E. H.|title=Energy, Heat and the Structure of Matter|last2=Ward|first2=A. H.|publisher=[[Thomas Nelson (publisher)|Nelson]]|year=1977|location=London|language=English}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|last1=Ward|first1=E. H.|title=Light and Sound|last2=Ward|first2=A. H.|publisher=[[Thomas Nelson (publisher)|Nelson]]|year=1977|location=London|language=English}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|last1=Ward|first1=E. H.|title=Magnetism, Electricity and Atomic Physics|last2=Ward|first2=A. H.|publisher=[[Thomas Nelson (publisher)|Nelson]]|year=1977|location=London|language=English}}</ref> This updated version later appeared as a single volume.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Ward|first=Elizabeth Honor|title=Essential senior physics in 51 units.|date=1980|publisher=Nelson|others=A. H. Ward|isbn=0-17-511496-X|edition=[New ed.]|location=Sunbury-on-Thames|oclc=16478165}}</ref>

== Personal life and death ==

Ward met Elizabeth Honor Shedden (12 April 1926 – 18 September 2016), also a physicist, at the University of Birmingham, and they married in 1950. They were both active in the Birmingham University Evangelical Christian Union, and remained active church members throughout their lives. Alan Ward died on 2 December 2021 at Groveland Care Home in Yeovil, Somerset. They had four children Kristina, Sheena, James, and [[Thomas Ward (mathematician)|Thomas]], whose [https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-3-031-39074-6 memoir]<ref>{{Cite book |last=Ward |first=Thomas |author-link=Thomas Ward (mathematician) |url=https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-3-031-39074-6 |title=People, places, and mathematics |publisher=[[Springer Nature]] |year=2023 |isbn=978-3-031-39073-9 |series=Springer Biographies |location=Cham |doi=10.1007/978-3-031-39074-6 |language=English}}</ref> has a more detailed account of Ward's life and work.
